This one was worth slowing down for, because my first instinct was wrong.

Two gauge fires looked contradictory: the plus flew **4** at step 74 and **5** at step 81 — same token, same gauge, same direction. I was one step from concluding the fire distance was situational and inventing yet another special case. Instead I diffed the two frames against the passability map, and the contradiction dissolved:

**Both fires threw v−1 = 4.** Step 81 only *looked* like 5 because its k=4 landing requires cell (4,6) — which sits inside the row-6 wall. So it legitimately overshot to k=5. The launch rule was never broken; it was doing exactly what it should.

That mattered enormously, because the model's predicted **plus position was already exactly right**. The sole error was T. Had I "fixed" the launch distance, I'd have broken a correct rule to explain an error it wasn't causing.

The real gap was narrower and more interesting:

> **A launch SWEEPS.** It shoves every token whose cells lie anywhere along the path it travels (k=1..K) — not just those in the final landing.

T was sitting at (3,7), a cell the plus merely *passed through* on its way from (4,3) to (4,8), and got pushed clear to (2,9),(3,9). My existing "first free passable spot" shove computed that displacement perfectly once the *trigger* was widened. One line, no new constants — and the model went to **391/391 across all levels**.

There's a nice asymmetry the level taught me: intermediate cells are ignored for **walls** (launches pierce them) but not for **tokens** (launches collect them). Both halves are now encoded.

36 actions to LEVEL_UP, n=117 against a 200 budget.
